questions.q: Where is a network intrusion detection system (NIDS) installed?
choices: On every end host, like antivirus software
Between the router and the internal network, so all traffic to and from the Internet passes through it
Inside each web server's logging subsystem
At the attacker's ISP
questions.explain: A NIDS sits between the router and the internal network, so it can see (and possibly modify) every packet going to or coming from the outside Internet.

questions.q: What is the biggest advantage of a NIDS?
choices: It can read TLS-encrypted traffic without any extra setup
It always interprets packets the same way the end host does
One NIDS covers the whole network, so it is cheap and needs little management
It detects attacks only after they finish, which avoids false positives
questions.explain: Every request passes through the NIDS, so a single install protects the whole network and nothing has to go on the end hosts.

questions.q: Which of these are real challenges for a NIDS?
choices: It has to split packets by connection and put them back in order by TCP sequence number before it can analyze them
It may see packets that never reach the end host (for example, the TTL runs out after the NIDS or the packet is dropped)
It cannot read HTTPS traffic unless end hosts give it their private keys
It must be installed separately on every machine in the network
It can only look at events after they have already happened
questions.explain: A NIDS has to rebuild TCP streams, reason about packets that may not arrive, and deal with end-to-end encryption. Installing on every machine is the HIDS drawback, and working only after the fact is the logging drawback.

questions.q: Why might the TCP connection a NIDS rebuilds differ from the one the end host actually receives?
choices: The NIDS may receive a packet whose TTL runs out before it reaches the end host, so the host throws it away
TCP packets are encrypted by default, so the NIDS sees only random bytes
The end host reorders packets by arrival time while the NIDS uses sequence numbers
Routers delete the TCP header before forwarding packets to the internal network
questions.explain: A packet can still be alive when it passes the NIDS and then expire (or get corrupted or dropped) before the end host gets it. So the NIDS has to reason about packets that might never arrive.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of a host-based IDS (HIDS) compared with a NIDS?
choices: It cannot see decrypted HTTPS traffic
It must be installed on every machine, possibly configured differently on each one, which can be very costly
It has more parsing inconsistencies than a NIDS
It can only run on logs after the fact
questions.explain: A HIDS runs on the end host itself, so you need one per machine. That costs much more than one NIDS for the whole network.

questions.q: To inspect HTTPS traffic, a HIDS must be given the end host's TLS private key.
questions.explain: A HIDS runs on the end host, so it can see the traffic after it has been decrypted. Needing private keys to inspect TLS is a NIDS problem.

questions.q: Antivirus software running on an employee's laptop is an example of a HIDS.
questions.explain: Antivirus runs on the same computer that sends and receives the network requests, which makes it a host-based detector.

questions.q: What is the biggest drawback of log-based intrusion detection?
choices: It is expensive, because servers need new software to produce logs
It cannot handle any kind of evasion attack
It cannot work in real time: an attack is found only after it has happened
It cannot see what files were accessed on the server
questions.explain: A log entry is written only after the event, so logging finds attacks after the fact. That is dangerous if the attack does damage right away, but late detection is still better than none.

questions.q: Logging is usually a cheap detection method, because web servers already log requests and the only extra cost is sometimes running a script over the logs.
questions.explain: Most web servers have logging built in, so the extra cost is small.

questions.q: Which detector types use information straight from the end host, avoiding many parsing inconsistencies and most encrypted-traffic problems?
choices: NIDS
HIDS
Logging
questions.explain: A HIDS and log analysis both work with what the end host actually received and processed. A NIDS sits in the middle of the network, so it has to guess how the host will read each packet and cannot see inside TLS.

questions.q: Nearly all of a company's traffic is HTTPS. It wants to inspect request contents in real time and does not want to share the servers' private keys with any other device. Which detector type fits best?
choices: NIDS
HIDS
Logging
None of these can inspect HTTPS
questions.explain: A HIDS sees the decrypted traffic on the host and works in real time. A NIDS would need the private keys, and logging is not real time.

questions.q: A company has thousands of different machines and mostly unencrypted traffic. It wants real-time detection with the lowest cost and management overhead. Which detector type fits best?
choices: NIDS
HIDS
Logging
A separately configured HIDS on each machine plus logging
questions.explain: One NIDS covers the whole network in real time, and unencrypted traffic removes its biggest weakness. A HIDS on thousands of different machines would be expensive, and logging is not real time.

questions.q: What is the name for an attack in which the attacker disguises the contents of an attack so a detector fails to recognize it?
questions.explain: In an evasion attack the attacker exploits differences between how the detector and the end host interpret the same data.

questions.q: A NIDS raises an alert whenever a request contains the string /etc/passwd. An attacker sends %65%74%63/%70%61%73%73%77%64 instead. Why does this get past the NIDS?
choices: The NIDS cannot read requests that contain percent signs
The string is encrypted with TLS
The NIDS does plain string matching, but the end host URL-decodes the input into /etc/passwd
The TTL of the packet expires before it reaches the NIDS
questions.explain: The detector and the end host interpret the bytes differently. A NIDS has to reason about how end hosts will decode what they receive, not just match raw strings.

questions.q: A web server serves files from /public/files based on a filename the user supplies. An attacker submits ../../etc/passwd to reach the password file. What is this type of attack called?
questions.explain: In Unix, .. means go up one directory, so the input escapes the intended directory and reaches /etc/passwd.

questions.q: To fully defend against path traversal attacks, what must a HIDS reason about beyond the contents of the request?
choices: The TTL values of the incoming packets
How the underlying filesystem interprets the requested path
The TLS private key of the server
The order of TCP sequence numbers
questions.explain: Whether a path is dangerous depends on how the filesystem resolves it (for example, ..). Modeling that adds new chances for parsing mismatches and evasion.

questions.q: Because a HIDS runs on the end host, it is immune to evasion attacks.
questions.explain: A HIDS has fewer inconsistency problems, but attacks like path traversal still require it to model how the filesystem interprets input, and that can still be evaded.

questions.q: Log-based detection still has to deal with evasion attacks such as path traversal, which require careful filesystem parsing.
questions.explain: Logs come from the end host, which avoids many parsing problems, but recognizing path traversal still means understanding how paths resolve.

questions.q: What is a false negative?
choices: No attack occurs, but the detector reports an attack
An attack occurs, but the detector reports no attack
An attack occurs, and the detector reports it
No attack occurs, and the detector reports nothing
questions.explain: A false negative is a missed attack, like a fire alarm that stays silent during a fire.

questions.q: A fire alarm goes off, but there is no fire. What kind of error is this?
choices: False positive
False negative
True positive
True negative
questions.explain: The detector reported an event (fire or attack) that did not happen.

questions.q: A detector reports an attack on every single input. Which statement is true?
choices: It has a 0% false positive rate
It has a 0% false negative rate, but it is useless
It has a 0% rate for both error types
Its error rates depend on the base rate of attacks
questions.explain: It can never miss an attack, so it has no false negatives. But it flags every benign input, so it is useless. In the same way, a detector that never alerts has a 0% false positive rate.

questions.q: In general, tuning a detector to lower its false positive rate tends to raise its false negative rate.
questions.explain: Fewer false positives means alerting less often, so the detector also misses more real attacks. Designing a detector means balancing the two error rates.

questions.q: Detector A has a 0.1% false positive rate and a 2% false negative rate. Detector B has a 2% false positive rate and a 0.1% false negative rate. For a building's fire alarm, which is probably better?
choices: A, because false positives waste the fire department's time
B, because a missed fire (false negative) costs far more than a false alarm
They are equally good, because their total error rates are equal
Neither, because any nonzero false negative rate is unacceptable
questions.explain: Which detector is better depends on what each kind of error costs. A missed fire means the building burns down, while a false alarm wastes an hour. If false positives were the more expensive error, A would be better.

questions.q: A detector has a 1% false positive rate. A site receives 50,000 requests per day, and 50 of them are attacks. How many false positives should you expect per day?
questions.explain: False positives can only come from benign requests: 1% x (50,000 - 50) = 1% x 49,950 = 499.5.

questions.q: A detector has a 0.5% false positive rate. A network sees 2,000,000 requests per day, and 20 of them are attacks. About how many false positives per day should you expect? (Round to the nearest whole number.)
questions.explain: 0.5% x (2,000,000 - 20) = 0.005 x 1,999,980 = 9,999.9, or about 10,000 alerts a day for only 20 real attacks.

questions.q: A detector has a 2% false negative rate. If 500 real attacks happen in a month, how many should you expect it to miss?
questions.explain: The false negative rate applies only to real attacks: 2% x 500 = 10 missed attacks.

questions.q: A detector's traffic grows from 1,000 to 10 million requests a day while the number of attacks stays at 5. Its false positive rate goes up, which is why it becomes less useful.
questions.explain: The rate (for example 0.1%) does not change. What changes is the number of false positives, from about 1 a day to about 10,000 a day, because the attack rate is now far lower. That is too many alerts to review.

questions.q: Even a very accurate detector can produce an unmanageable flood of false alarms when real attacks are extremely rare. What is this phenomenon called?
choices: The evasion problem
The base rate fallacy
Path traversal
Specification drift
questions.explain: When attacks are a tiny fraction of the traffic, even a small false positive rate times a huge number of benign events produces far more false alarms than real attacks.

questions.q: Which detection strategy looks for activity that matches the structure of a known attack, which amounts to blacklisting?
choices: Signature-based
Anomaly-based
Specification-based
Behavioral
questions.explain: Signature-based detection keeps a list of disallowed patterns and flags anything that matches one.

questions.q: A detector flags any input that has the pattern 'garbage bytes, then a memory address, then shellcode', the usual shape of a buffer overflow exploit. Which strategy is this?
choices: Behavioral
Specification-based
Signature-based
Anomaly-based
questions.explain: It matches input against the known structure of an attack, which makes it a signature.

questions.q: Which are drawbacks of signature-based detection?
choices: It will not catch new attacks that have no known signature
It may miss variants of known attacks that differ enough from the signature
Detecting known signatures is computationally hard
It can only detect an attack after the exploit has already run
questions.explain: Signatures are easy to check and very good against known attacks, but new attacks and modified variants can slip past. Detecting only after the exploit runs is a drawback of behavioral detection.

questions.q: A system trains a statistical model on a month of past traffic and flags any request that differs significantly from it. Which strategy is this?
choices: Signature-based
Anomaly-based
Specification-based
Behavioral
questions.explain: Anomaly-based detection learns a model of normal activity (a whitelist) and flags anything that deviates from it.

questions.q: What is the key difference between specification-based and anomaly-based detection?
choices: Specification-based uses blacklisting; anomaly-based uses whitelisting
Specification-based defines normal activity by hand; anomaly-based learns a model of normal activity
Specification-based only runs on logs; anomaly-based only runs on a NIDS
Specification-based looks at program behavior; anomaly-based looks at known attack patterns
questions.explain: Both are whitelisting: they flag what falls outside normal activity. They differ in whether a person writes the definition of normal or a model learns it.

questions.q: A programmer knows an age field should only ever contain a number, and configures the detector to flag any non-numeric input to that field. Which strategy is this?
choices: Specification-based
Anomaly-based
Signature-based
Behavioral
questions.explain: Normal behavior was written down by hand, so this is specification-based detection.

questions.q: A program never legitimately calls exec. The detector raises an alert whenever the program calls exec, without examining the input at all. Which strategy is this?
choices: Signature-based
Anomaly-based
Specification-based
Behavioral
questions.explain: Behavioral detection looks for evidence of compromise (the result of the exploit, such as spawning a shell), not for attack patterns in the input.

questions.q: Which detection strategies can catch new attacks that have never been seen before?
choices: Signature-based
Anomaly-based
Specification-based
Behavioral
questions.explain: Anomaly-based, specification-based and behavioral detection do not need prior knowledge of a specific attack. Signature-based detection only catches attacks whose signatures are already known.

questions.q: Anomaly-based detection is the most widely deployed detection strategy in practice.
questions.explain: Anomaly-based detection is mostly studied in academic papers and is not widely deployed.

questions.q: Which is a specific risk of anomaly-based detection?
choices: If the training data contains attacks, the model may learn to treat those attacks as normal
It cannot detect any attack that has not been seen before
It requires writing a manual specification for every application
It can only detect an attack after the exploit has run
questions.explain: Defining normal is hard. A model trained on data that includes attacks, or a poorly built model, can call attacks normal or flag lots of normal requests.

questions.q: What is the main drawback of specification-based detection?
choices: It has an unavoidably high false positive rate
It cannot catch new attacks
Writing specifications by hand for every application takes a lot of time
It only detects attacks after they have started
questions.explain: Specification-based detection can catch new attacks, and a well-defined spec can make false positives very rare, but writing specs by hand is very time-consuming.

questions.q: Which are drawbacks of behavioral detection?
choices: The attack is detected only after it has started, so it cannot be prevented beforehand
An attacker can avoid detection by using different behavior to carry out the attack
It is always expensive to implement
It cannot catch never-before-seen attacks
questions.explain: Behavioral detection can be cheap, can catch new attacks, and has few false positives when the watched behavior almost never happens legitimately. But it reacts only once the compromise is underway, and attackers can switch to other behavior.

questions.q: Behavioral detection works by scanning the attacker's input for malicious patterns.
questions.explain: Behavioral detection ignores the input and watches what the program does (for example, an unexpected exec call), looking for the result of the exploit.

questions.q: In NSA terminology, what is a 'selector'?
choices: A piece of malicious code planted on a target's machine
A piece of information that identifies what you are looking for, such as an email address or phone number
An intrusion detection match
A wiretap installed at an overseas fiber link
questions.explain: Selectors are identifiers such as email addresses and phone numbers. A 'fingerprint' is an intrusion detection match, and an 'implant' is malcode or other sabotage.

questions.q: In NSA terminology, what is a 'fingerprint'?
choices: An intrusion detection match
A user's biometric login data
A piece of malcode or sabotage
An email address being searched for
questions.explain: A fingerprint is an intrusion detection match, for example one that identifies an application or how it is being used.

questions.q: In NSA terminology, what is the word for a piece of malcode or other sabotage?
questions.explain: An implant is malcode or another piece of sabotage.

questions.q: Under section 702 of the FISA Amendments Act, the NSA can obtain all of a person's information through a US provider when that person is:
choices: A US citizen located outside the United States
A permanent resident located inside the United States
Not a US person (not a citizen or permanent resident) and located outside the United States
Anyone who communicates through a US provider
questions.explain: Section 702 covers non-US persons outside the US. Someone who is a US person, or who is located inside the US, gets much more protection under the Constitution.

questions.q: Which countries are members of the Five Eyes (FVEY) intelligence alliance?
choices: Australia
Canada
Germany
New Zealand
United Kingdom
France
United States
questions.explain: The Five Eyes are Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK and the US, which are parties to the UKUSA agreement on signals intelligence.

questions.q: The primary rule within the Five Eyes alliance is 'when in country X, behave according to country X's laws'.
questions.explain: That is the stated primary rule among the UKUSA partners.

questions.q: Why does the NSA's goal of collecting all relevant communications for valid targets lead it to collect data on everyone?
choices: The law requires it to collect on US persons too
A valid target could be anyone, so it needs global capability, and it stores everything it can in case it is needed later
Collecting everything lowers its false positive rate
Encrypted traffic can only be decrypted if it is collected in bulk
questions.explain: Since anyone could turn out to be a target, it collects and keeps whatever it can. The downside is that there is now so much data that finding the relevant details is much harder.

questions.q: From a technical point of view, what are the NSA's Xkeyscore Deepdive wiretaps?
choices: Host-based intrusion detection systems installed on targets' computers
Scalable network intrusion detection systems that parse traffic and store the extracted metadata
Log analysis scripts run on US providers' web servers
Behavioral detectors that watch for exec calls
questions.explain: They are NIDS at large scale: they pull in network traffic, parse packets to extract metadata, and store it in a dataframe, with pre-made fingerprints and canned searches.

questions.q: According to the material, what is the simplest way to evade Xkeyscore-style bulk monitoring?
choices: Send packets with very low TTL values
URL-encode sensitive strings
Encrypt the data with good transport cryptography
Use path traversal in your requests
questions.explain: Unlike with a conventional NIDS, encrypting the data is enough to evade this monitoring. Good transport cryptography causes the NSA significant collection problems.

questions.q: What does the NSA do with encrypted traffic its wiretaps cannot read?
choices: Discards it immediately
Sends it to a black box elsewhere, usually in a datacenter, in case the key is obtained later and the ciphertext can be decrypted
Forwards it to the end host's HIDS for analysis
Re-encrypts it with its own key and sends it on
questions.explain: Encrypted traffic is collected and stored. If the key is obtained later, the stored ciphertext can be turned back into plaintext.
